text: Every system you've secured so far draws a hard line between code and data. SQL has one. Web routing has one. Large language models don't — and that single fact is why prompt injection exists at all. This lesson is about direct prompt injection specifically: the simplest version, where the attacker is just the end user, typing into the same box every legitimate customer uses.

Here's the architectural reason it works. Everything the model receives — the developer's system prompt, the user's message, any retrieved content — arrives as one undifferentiated stream of tokens. The model predicts the next most likely token from everything in that window. Nothing inherently tells it the developer's instructions outrank text that simply looks like an instruction. OWASP ranks this as LLM01 — the top entry in its Top 10 for LLM Applications — for exactly that reason.

In practice, a direct injection attempt is text crafted so the model treats part of it as a new, higher-priority command instead of as content to respond to. The attacker needs no elevated access and no special tooling. They need the ordinary chat box, phrased to assert authority it was never given.

You don't defend against this by memorizing exact attack strings — new phrasings appear constantly. What holds up is recognizing the shape: messages that claim new authority over the conversation, that ask the model to reveal its own hidden configuration, or that use role-play and hypothetical framing specifically to route around a refusal the model was configured to hold.

And the stakes change entirely once that model can act — applying credits, writing to a repository, calling an internal API. Direct injection against a model like that isn't just an odd reply; it's natural language used as the exploit payload for a real action nobody authorized. Next lesson goes further still: the attacker doesn't even need to type anything — only to plant the right text somewhere the model will later read.
